readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 7:1-28, and if you can, reread Genesis 14:17-20 first. The argument here is dense, so read it twice if needed. The core claim is simple: if perfection had been possible through the Levitical priesthood, there would have been no need for another priest to arise.
settingTheScene: Last week the author mentioned Melchizedek and then paused to rebuke his readers. Now he returns to the subject and gives it a full chapter. Why does this obscure figure from Genesis matter so much? Because he is the key to understanding how Jesus, who descended from the tribe of Judah and not Levi, can serve as a priest at all. The readers were Jewish Christians who revered the Levitical priesthood as God’s own institution. The author does not belittle it. He shows that Scripture itself, in Genesis 14 and Psalm 110, pointed beyond it. This chapter argues that the old priesthood was a temporary shadow, and that the permanent reality has come in Christ.
observation: Melchizedek is “king of righteousness” and “king of peace,” king of Salem and priest of God Most High (vv. 1-2).
He is described as “without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God” (v. 3).
Abraham gave him a tenth of the spoils, and Melchizedek blessed Abraham. “It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior” (v. 7).
Levi, still in the loins of Abraham, paid tithes through him (vv. 9-10).
If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, why would another priest arise “after the order of Melchizedek” (v. 11)?
A change of priesthood requires a change of law (v. 12), and Jesus descended from Judah, a tribe with no priestly role (v. 14).
Jesus became a priest “by the power of an indestructible life” and not by ancestry (v. 16).
“He always lives to make intercession for them” (v. 25), and he is “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (v. 26).
interpretation:
This chapter is an exercise in careful Bible reading. The author takes a few verses of Genesis and a single line of Psalm 110 and draws out their full implications. His argument has three steps.

First, Melchizedek is greater than Abraham. Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing. In ancient culture, the one who blesses is superior, and the one who tithes is inferior. Since Levi descended from Abraham, the whole Levitical priesthood, in a sense, tithed to Melchizedek in Abraham. So Melchizedek’s priesthood has a greater standing than Aaron’s.

Second, the very existence of the Melchizedek priest in Psalm 110, centuries after Moses, shows that the Levitical system was incomplete. If the old priesthood could bring perfection, meaning a full and lasting cleansing of conscience and access to God, then no one would have needed to speak of a different priest. But God did speak of one. A new priesthood implies a new law, because the priesthood and the law are tied together. And that is exactly what the new covenant is. The author is not saying the law was bad, but that it was provisional, preparing for something better.

Third, Jesus is that priest. His qualification is not ancestry but “the power of an indestructible life.” The Levitical priests died and were replaced, one after another. Jesus lives forever, and therefore his priesthood does not pass to anyone else. Verse 24 says “he holds his priesthood permanently.” The practical result is verse 25: “he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.” This is one of the most comforting verses in the New Testament. Uttermost means completely, to the end. The saving power of Christ does not run out, and his intercession does not stop.

What about the description of Melchizedek as having no father, mother, or genealogy? The author is not saying that Melchizedek was a mysterious immortal. He is reading the silence of Genesis. The narrative gives no parentage and records no death. Therefore, as presented in Scripture, he resembles the eternal Son of God. He is a type, a living picture drawn by the Holy Spirit, and the original is Christ.

Verses 26-28 sum it up. We needed a high priest who is holy, innocent, and unstained, who has no need to offer sacrifices for his own sins first, and who offered one sacrifice once for all when he offered up himself. The old priests had to offer for themselves and then for the people, day after day. Jesus did it once, and it was enough.
connection: The backbone of this chapter is Genesis 14:17-20 and Psalm 110:4. The tithe and blessing look back to Genesis 12:2-3 and forward to the new covenant in Hebrews 8. The Levitical priesthood was established in Exodus 28-29 and Leviticus 8-9. Isaiah 53:12 pictures the Servant who makes intercession for transgressors, and Romans 8:34 gives the same truth about Christ’s present ministry.
application:
First, take comfort in “to the uttermost.” If you suspect that your sin or weakness is too much for Christ, this verse says otherwise. He saves completely and perpetually.

Second, let the phrase “he always lives to make intercession” shape your prayers. When you do not know what to say, remember that someone is already speaking for you.

Third, notice that Hebrews treats the Old Testament as a book about Christ. Next time you come across a puzzling Old Testament passage, ask: how might this point forward to Jesus? You may not always find the answer, but the question will make you a better reader.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he is your priest forever and always lives to pray for you.
Tell him what you need him to intercede for.
Thank him that he saves you to the uttermost.
